title: Ladino
hookLine: Judeo-Spanish, the language of the Sephardi diaspora

cards: A grandmother in Istanbul tucks a child into bed and sings a lullaby. The words are Spanish, almost. Someone from Madrid would catch half of it and stumble on the rest.
Hebrew words are woven through it, and Turkish ones, and on an old printed page the whole song might be spelled in Hebrew letters.
That lullaby came a very long way to reach that bedroom, in people's mouths, not in a suitcase. Today's word is the name of the language it's sung in: Ladino.

teach.b: Ladino is Judeo-Spanish: the Spanish that Jews carried with them when they were expelled from Spain, and kept speaking, generation after generation, far from Spain.
Families settled across the Ottoman lands, in cities like Salonika, Istanbul, Izmir and Sarajevo, and the language went with them. Start with the name of the people who spoke it.

The prophet Obadiah, in a single verse, speaks of exiles of Jerusalem living in a place called Sepharad. Nobody can say for sure what place Obadiah meant. But Jewish tradition came to read Sepharad as Spain.
So the Jews of Spain became Sephardim, the people of Sepharad, and Ladino became the language of the Sephardi diaspora. Now the language itself.
Back in Spain, Spanish kept changing. Ladino went its own way. Speakers of modern Spanish sometimes say it sounds like an older book come to life.
And it picked up new neighbors' words as it went: Hebrew for holy things, Turkish and Greek and others for the market and the street. A few words to taste. Kerido, or kerida: dear.

teach.h: A SONG IN A FOREIGN LAND.
teach.b: A psalm asks how anyone can sing the Lord's song in a foreign land.
Ladino is one people's answer: you sing it in the language you carried. Ballads, proverbs, wedding songs, lullabies and prayers for home, passed from grandmother to grandchild.
Today far fewer families speak Ladino at home, and teachers, singers and writers are working to keep it in the world. Every song they keep is a little bit of Sepharad, still traveling.

how: Sephardi families and synagogues keep Ladino alive in songs, proverbs and some prayers and readings, and today there are classes, choirs and recordings devoted to it.

games.q: your family has been expelled from Spain and settles in a new city in the Ottoman lands. what language do you speak at home?
o: only the language of the new city.
the Spanish you carried, with new words woven in.
games.why: Sephardi families kept their Spanish, and it grew into Ladino, taking in Hebrew, Turkish and Greek words along the way.

practice: Take the word kerido, or kerida: dear. Breathe in and let one face come to mind, someone dear to you; breathe out, and say the word for them, in your head or under your breath.
